World.title: WUF13 in Baku hosts key dialogue on housing and post-crisis recovery
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, May 21. As part of the fifth day of the 13th session of the World Urban Forum (WUF13) in Baku, a dialogue is being held on the topic “Housing at the Centre of Crisis Recovery and Reconstruction,” Trend reports.

The event will discuss measures to address the crisis in cities affected by conflict, the consequences of climate change and natural disasters, as well as the key role of housing in recovery and reconstruction processes.

In addition, it is reported that the session will emphasize the importance of providing safe and affordable housing in the context of the growing influx of internally displaced persons and other vulnerable groups into cities.

The discussion will focus on how governments, local communities, and the private sector can collaborate in the recovery of settlements and neighborhoods, as well as on the importance of protecting housing, land, and property rights.

The event will explore practical approaches to supporting population resilience, safe return or resettlement, and promoting sustainable and inclusive urban regeneration, drawing on experiences of conflict-induced displacement and post-crisis recovery.

Meanwhile, the session is expected to conclude with a call for the creation of a new platform for cooperation that will prioritize the reconstruction of housing and neighborhoods, as well as scalable solutions to the problem of internal displacement, and ensure the active participation of local communities.

Today marks the fifth day of WUF13 in Baku.

The first day included a ministerial meeting dedicated to the New Urban Agenda, a ministerial roundtable, assemblies for women and civil society, business sessions, and discussions on urban prosperity. An official ceremony marking the raising of the UN and Azerbaijani flags also took place.

The second day stood out for the inaugural Leaders' Summit, featuring high-level discussions on the global housing crisis, urbanization policy, and urban resilience. Concurrently, the opening of the Mexico City pavilion took place, serving as a significant platform for expanding cooperation with the Latin American region and preparing for WUF14.

The third day of WUF13 featured a comprehensive program of events covering the global housing crisis, the formation of safe and inclusive cities, climate resilience, artificial intelligence and urban governance, green urbanization, social equity, and sustainable transport.

One of the highlights of the third day was the signing of a sister-city memorandum between the Azerbaijani city of Shusha and the Turkish city of Trabzon.

The fourth day of WUF13 featured a broad program of events dedicated to urbanization, climate change, inclusive urban development, housing policy, and sustainable governance.

One of the important events of the UN Special Program for the Economies of Central Asia (SPECA) Cities Forum, held on the fourth day, was the announcement of Almaty’s official accession to the “Declaration of Intent on the Establishment of the SPECA Smart Climate-Resilient Cities Forum.”

Also, for the first time in WUF history and at Azerbaijan’s initiative, the “WUF13 NGO Forum: Global Partnership and Decision-Making” was held.

WUF13, which has attracted more than 40,000 registered participants from 182 countries, will continue until May 22. Held under the theme “Housing the world: Safe and resilient cities and communities,” the forum brings together governments, international organizations, experts, and representatives of civil society to strengthen global cooperation in the field of sustainable urban development.

Will be updated

World.title: Man with 'very serious' criminal history jailed over motorcyclist's death
World.content:
Allan John Eveleigh has been sentenced to three-and-a-half years in jail after pleading guilty to killing a "much-loved" family man in Toowoomba in 2023.

The court was told the 56-year-old Everleigh had had a "very high" level of methamphetamine in his blood when he failed to stop at a traffic light on Bridge Street in Cotswold Hills early on June 21.

Allan Eveleigh will spend the next 10 months behind bars before being eligible for parole. (Supplied)

The truck he was driving collided with the back of Ian "Watty" Welldon's motorcycle as he waited at the lights at the intersection of Bridge and Nugent Pinch Road.

Mr Welldon died at the scene.

Eveleigh pleaded guilty in the Toowoomba District Court to one count of dangerous operation of a motor vehicle causing death, nearly three years after the crash but before the matter went to trial.

Mr Welldon's wife, Cherie, and two adult children, Chais and Ilannah, read powerful victim impact statements in court, describing how their lives had been irrevocably changed by the tragedy.

Ilannah (left), Cherie (centre) and Chais Welldon read powerful victim impact statements to the court. (ABC Southern Queensland: Dan McCray)

Cherie Welldon told the court that her husband's death had changed the rhythm of her breathing, the way food tasted and robbed her of her sense of purpose in life.

"He's my best friend, my soulmate, my rock," Mrs Welldon said.

She also told the court of the financial strain caused by her husband's death.

"I have no future. It seems dark," she said.

Ilannah Welldon said the day of the crash was the last day her dad had been planning to ride to work that winter.

"The next day he would have been driving my car," she said.

"I know kids are always supposed to outlive their parents, but that shouldn't have happened two months before [my] 23rd birthday."

Ian Welldon would regularly participate in charity motorcycle rides and had plans to travel around Australia with his family. (Supplied: Welldon family)

Chais Welldon said he had lost his mentor.

"He was the person I went to for advice on everything, from relationships to work to our hobbies. He was my father, my best friend," he said.

Judge Jennifer Rosengren described the tragedy as "nothing short of extreme" and said sentencing in such cases was one of the hardest parts of her job.

During sentencing, Judge Rosengren read aloud Eveleigh's criminal and traffic history and said that while it did not aggravate the penalty she handed down, it was relevant.

Eveleigh had a long traffic history, including convictions for drink and drug driving, as well as a criminal history the prosecution described as deplorable, which included convictions for home invasion and sexual assault.

Judge Rosengren did, however, accept that Eveleigh had shown genuine remorse, both at the scene when he rendered first aid to Mr Welldon and afterwards, when he asked his lawyer to pass on his apology to Mr Welldon's family in court.

She emphasised that Eveleigh's offending was not a case of "momentary inattention", noting the traffic light had been red for 14 to 15 seconds before he crashed into the back of Mr Welldon's motorcycle.

She said that while there was no medical evidence to confirm Eveleigh had been affected by the methamphetamine in his system, he was willing to put other road users at risk by driving while knowing it was present.

She also said that, due to his history, she regarded his prospects of rehabilitation "more conservatively".

He was sentenced to three-and-a-half years behind bars, with a parole eligibility period of 10 months.

Outside court, Mr Welldon's family said the sentence did not bring them any closure.

"He pretty much got away with it," Chais Welldon said.

World.title: Blues fighting for an Origin dynasty a decade in the making
World.content:
The last time Isabelle Kelly played for New South Wales on the Gold Coast, she helped end a dynasty. Now she's trying to cement one.

The Blues captain has a chance to lead her side to the first 3-0 whitewash in women's State of Origin history in next Thursday's clash.

A win would put a capstone on back-to-back series wins where Kelly's side has not lost a live match and give the Blues a fair claim to being the most dominant side in women's Origin history.

But Kelly, one of the side's longest-serving players, has never forgotten what it's like to be on the other side of a legend.

Ten years ago, the last time New South Wales and Queensland met at Skilled Park, Kelly was a 19-year-old winger who played her part in the Blues' 8-4 victory in the old interstate challenge.

Isabelle Kelly (sixth from right in back row) was part of New South Wales's breakthrough win in 2016. (NRL Photos)

"I was in awe of all the Blues players but I didn't know any of the Queenslanders," Kelly said.

"I got in a scuffle with Ali Brigginshaw, but I didn't know who Ali Brigginshaw was. We laugh about it now."

It was New South Wales's first ever win over the Maroons since the first meeting of the two sides in 1999 and players wept on the field after ending their 17-year losing run.

Women's rugby league has come a long way since, especially since the interstate clash officially came under the Origin banner in 2018, but Kelly has never forgotten the power of that victory.

"I remember the older girls talking about it all the time, talking about the pain. They still hurt — they still talk about much it hurt to lose for that long, but they kept going, they kept turning up and they helped us get to this position we're in now," Kelly said.

Why there's no end in sight for Origin's ageless wonder Kezie Apps will be the oldest State of Origin player across both states and the men's and women's series this year, but the 35-year-old Blues stalwart shows no signs of slowing down.

"It helped create me as a player, learning what they'd been through and how they had the determination to play even if things weren't going their way or women's sport wasn't on the map.

"I'll always carry winning that game with me, because of what it meant to those girls."

Alongside fellow veteran Kezie Apps and bench utility Corban Baxter, the Roosters flyer will return to the site of their triumph 10 years later as the Blues try and put the finishing touches on a dominant run of their own.

It's the second year in a row John Strange's side has had a whitewash at their mercy and the memory of last year's dead rubber defeat in Newcastle has acted as driving force throughout this series.

Isabelle Kelly and Kezie Apps are New South Wales's longest-serving players. (AAP Images: Darren England)

"Nobody wants to hold the shield up after losing. It's just not the same feeling. A lot of us take it personally when we lose, we feel like we've let people down and let the state down," Kelly said.

"Even before we came into our six-week block that was something we spoke about. We let ourselves down, we didn't play to what we know we can. It's a massive drive.

"We have spoken about it just as a reminder of that feeling of failure. We won't bring it up every day but it's a fuel that adds to the determination you have every day.

"You have to fix it right up."

Kelly's confidence is rooted in her belief that the Blues' best football could still be yet to come.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

They've relied on defence and power running to get them home in the first two matches and Kelly believes a greater fluency awaits in Game III, where they'll be warm favourites against the injury-hit Queenslanders.

"We know where we can [be] better, mainly in attack. We haven't showcased what we can," Kelly said.

"We're really calm, really confident, but we have this grit as well. We can go up there and ice it.

"When you pull on this jersey it's such a unique opportunity and it's something you might never get again. For us to be able to fix what happened last year is really exciting."

World.title: NDIS whistleblower protections 'among worst in the country', inquiry told
World.content:
A support worker cut keys to a deafblind National Disability Insurance Scheme (NDIS) participant's home without their knowledge, a parliamentary inquiry has been told.

The claim was one of a raft of concerns raised today at an inquiry into the scheme's integrity, with evidence also given that many people with disability do not formally report misconduct due to a perception the scheme's watchdog is a "toothless tiger".

The work of the NDIS watchdog and provider complaints body, the Quality and Safeguards Commission (QSC), and whistleblower protections were among several topics discussed at length.

Will drastic NDIS overhaul repeat the mistakes of the past? The states are once again on the hook for disability services due to the Commonwealth's drastic NDIS cuts. Can the mistakes of the past be avoided?

Deafblind Australia told the committee that deafblind NDIS participants routinely reported, "feeling like an ATM" and providers were "primarily interested in … retaining the highest possible percentage of a person's plan, rather than assisting them to achieve [their goals]".

The inquiry also heard a deafblind participant unknowingly had keys to their home cut by a support worker.

The group's Ben McAtamney told the hearing many deafblind participants did not "see a point" in formally reporting misconduct due to a lack of faith anything would be done.

" There is definitely a feeling across the community that the Quality and Safeguards Commission is largely a toothless tiger. You report things, you make your complaint, but nothing ever changes. "

In addition, Mr McAtamney said the complaints processes were not accessible to deafblind people, which prevented or dissuaded them from making complaints.

"There is a bit of hesitance from the community to approach those formal pathways, maybe because of negative experiences in the past … but also … they don't feel cared about or wanted."

Disability Advocacy Network Australia's David Petherick said it was common to see "brave" people with disability "give up" on pursuing their complaints or never hear back about what came of them.

He said an effective complaints system that people with disability felt confident in was critical for the NDIS.

"We desperately want the QSC to succeed … but we recognise they are managing overwhelming demands in the constraints of their budget and the legislation."

Disability Advocacy Network Australia's David Petherick said it was common to see people with disability "give up" on pursuing their complaints. (ABC News: Patrick Stone)

The cross-party parliamentary committee has already heard about $3.7 billion was lost to "integrity leakage" last financial year, that the scheme was set up without robust payment guardrails, and sophisticated organised crime groups operating overseas were increasingly exploiting government programs, including the NDIS.

The NDIS has been projected to cost more than $50 billion this financial year, with increasing reports of widespread fraud, particularly from providers, leading to this inquiry.

Fraud is not a major driver of the scheme's overall growth, though it remains a key target for the Albanese government.

Major cuts to the NDIS were announced last month, with about 300,000 people with disability to either be kicked off or prevented from accessing the scheme over the next four years, saving more than $36 billion over that time.

The legislation required to enact those changes, which has been slammed by the Greens and disability community, has been referred to the Senate for a separate inquiry with a reporting date of June 16.

The bill also includes measures to plug gaps in oversight and require more providers to register with the scheme, while also allowing more automated decision-making and giving federal minister Mark Butler sweeping powers to cut certain types of supports.

Calls for whistleblower protections

The Human Rights Law Centre's Whistleblower Project used today's integrity hearing to renew calls to bolster NDIS whistleblowers protections, which it said was among the "worst in the country".

Despite some improvements in recent months, the project's Madeleine Howel said the laws remained inadequate.

"Whistleblowers play a critical role in exposing wrongdoing, ensuring there is integrity in the NDIS," she said.

Ex-Labor powerbroker's warning amid NDIS cuts A former NSW Labor powerbroker and state disability minister pivotal in advocating for the establishment of the NDIS has warned against rushing through sweeping changes to the scheme.

"Improving the regulatory and enforcement powers of regulators … will not alone strengthen the integrity of the NDIS."

In the December 2025 quarter, about 94 per cent of all NDIS providers were unregistered, meaning the scheme watchdog had little to no oversight of them.

The government has trumpeted the upcoming expansion of mandatory provider registration requirements as a key measure to crack down on fraud.

Groups representing allied health professionals told the hearing that could benefit large organisations and lock out smaller businesses or drive them away from the sector due to the high costs and administrative burden.

The prospect of mandatory provider registration was first raised in a review of the scheme ordered by former minister Bill Shorten, and views on it differ across the disability community.

World.title: What you need to know about tomorrow's ACT public school strike
World.content:
For the first time in 15 years, public school teachers and staff in the ACT are going on strike.

The two-hour work stoppage will see all public schools, including specialist schools and preschools, keep their doors closed until 10:30am on Friday, May 22.

Here's everything you need to know.

Why is this strike happening?

There's been mounting frustration between the Australian Education Union (AEU) and the Education Directorate as part of negotiations on a new enterprise agreement.

As part of the bargaining process, union members voted to take protected industrial action, and this strike is part of that action.

The union has 4,200 members, and the majority of ACT public school staff are expected to participate in the work stoppage.

The strike is the first coordinated stop-work action by ACT educators in 15 years. (ABC News: Adam Shirley)

The union's ACT branch president Angela Burroughs said public school staff felt "fed up".

"Teachers don't like doing this, but we are exhausted," she said.

" We are putting up with the unacceptable … our members' patience has expired. "

The union said teachers were taking this action because the government hadn't addressed core concerns around staffing, increasing workloads and class sizes.

What's the advice to parents and carers?

The director-general of the Education Directorate Jo Wood said alternatives were considered, but the decision to close schools was made "in the interest of student and staff safety".

"We weren't in a position to plan for a safe supervision environment for students," she said.

" It is not a decision taken lightly. "

As a result, the school day will begin at 10:30am, and parents and carers are being warned the later start will likely result in congestion around schools.

The Education Directorate said parents should have already received information from their child's schools about specific arrangements relating to the industrial action.

Jo Wood of the Community Services Directorate says the decision to close schools was not taken lightly. (ABC News: Monte Bovill)

Are school buses running?

School buses are running, but on their normal schedule.

The directorate said Transport Canberra couldn't change school bus services in time to accommodate a later school start time.

What about out-of-school care?

Some out-of-school care providers, who provide before-school care on public school sites, have been able to extend their hours.

Those providers should have already contacted parents and carers directly.

Will there be more strikes?

Friday's strike is part of the union's first phase of action, which also includes a ban on written student report comments and campaign messaging embedded in email signatures.

If the first round of actions fails to secure "meaningful progress" from the government, the union said it would escalate to a more extensive and disruptive second phase.

That could include full-day strikes.

Angela Burroughs of the Australian Education Union says more industrial action is likely if negotiations don't improve. (ABC News: Monte Bovill)

Ms Burroughs said more action was "highly likely".

"It's like negotiating with cardboard cutouts," she said.

" The government can prevent further industrial action at any time by coming to the table with an offer that actually addresses the issues educators are raising. "

Ms Wood said the directorate was now meeting with the union weekly.

"It is moving in the right direction," she said.

"We are continuing to progress on some claims and there are some others we still need to work through."

Education Minister Yvette Berry says she supports school staff taking protected industrial action. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

What does the minister have to say?

ACT Education Minister Yvette Berry said she supported teachers and school staff taking protected industrial action.

"I understand that this decision will be disruptive to the routine of many Canberrans," she said in a statement.

"I will continue to meet with the AEU as regularly and frequently as necessary to get a positive outcome."

World.title: Public transport to remain free in Tasmania for an additional year
World.content:
Public transport across Tasmania will remain free for an additional 12 months, in a move aimed at easing cost-of-living pressures.

The extension was confirmed in the state budget announced today, with the state government committing $24 million towards keeping fares free until July 2027.

Premier Jeremy Rockliff said the decision was made as a result of the popularity of the three-month trial of free public transport launched in late March.

Free public transport was set to end on July 1, but that's now being extended. (ABC News: Maren Preuss)

He said the number of people catching Metro buses had increased by about 37 per cent, while rides on Kinetic services had jumped by about 46 per cent.

"That's a significant … vote of confidence when it comes to public transport services and the cost of living measure of free public transport," Mr Rockliff said.

" This is a significant investment but, in my view, a worthy investment. "

Government to slash 1,700 jobs as Abetz looks to rein in Tasmanian spending The Tasmanian government will slash 1,700 jobs through natural attrition and negotiated voluntary redundancies, as Treasurer Eric Abetz unveils his second state budget.

The premier said it hoped the initiative would help Tasmanians save money, while also reducing traffic on the state's roads.

The free public transport includes travel on any bus that is not a private charter, as well as the Derwent Ferry service.

'We're not wasting time tapping our card'

Mount Stuart resident Catherine Udovicic catches the bus two or three times each week and said the additional year of free travel would be "absolutely marvellous".

She said the removal of fares had given her more freedom and she has also felt that the quality of services had improved.

Bus regular Catherine Udovicic is excited that free public transport will be extended. (ABC News: Monty Jacka)

"People can just jump on really quickly, we're not wasting time tapping our card or paying money, we just get straight on the bus and we're on the way," Ms Udovicic said.

"My sister, who lives on the north-west coast, was able to come down here and visit her grandchildren, stay a few days, and then go back because the bus was free."

Another supporter of the initiative was bus driver Leone Burston, who has worked for Metro Tasmania for about 20 years.

She said there had been "heaps more people" on the buses since fares were scrapped, including more families and older Tasmanians during non-peak periods.

"They're getting out to where they need to be. To their appointments, meeting friends for coffee and things like that," Ms Burston said.

Metro bus driver Leone Burston said more people are catching the bus. (ABC News: Monty Jacka)

The bus driver said not having to collect fares had also made her job easier, while also improving the mood of her passengers.

"They're happier because they're not having to find that extra money to be able to go out and meet their friends and do other enjoyment activities," she said.

"They feel a lot safer and we're going great guns with getting them where they need to go."

Free public transport was set to end on July 1, but that's now being extended. (ABC News: Monty Jacka)

Initiative could help keep older Tasmanians connected, minister says

Where are the cuts coming from in Tasmania's state budget? Treasurer Eric Abetz wants to find $1.47 billion in "efficiencies" in Tasmania's state budget. This is what's on the chopping block.

Bridget Archer, who is the state's Minister for Ageing, said it was also hoped the expanded initiative would help older people stay connected.

"For senior Tasmanians this can be a great way to get around … not just in the cities but right into regional Tasmania," Ms Archer said.

Ms Archer said it was important, especially when there are cost-of-living pressures, to ensure older people were "not cut off from their communities".

Mr Rockliff said the state government would look at potentially expanding the free public transport program over the next 12 months.

World.title: Defence minister 'disappointed' by lawsuit over Darwin port ownership
World.content:
Australia's minister for defence says the government will "do everything" in its power to defend an international lawsuit brought by the owners of Darwin port.

Richard Marles said he was "disappointed" in the steps taken by Chinese-owned company Landbridge but was unable to provide certainty around whether a domestic buyer had been secured.

At last year's federal election, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese pledged Labor would return the port to Australian hands, saying it was necessary for national security.

It was an election promise of Anthony Albanese's to return Darwin Port to Australian hands. (ABC News: Stuart Carnegie)

The government has since been locked in negotiations with Landbridge as it tries to secure an Australian buyer and has flagged it would be willing to force the company to hand over the asset if necessary.

Landbridge launched legal action to try and stop the federal government from stripping them of the asset earlier this month, arguing the government's move was "discriminatory" and breaks Australia's obligations under its free trade pact with Beijing.

Chinese company launches legal action over forced sale of Port of Darwin Anthony Albanese pledged at the federal election that Labor would return the port to Australian hands, saying it was necessary for national security.

During a visit to Darwin on Thursday, Mr Marles re-asserted the government's commitment to returning the port to a domestic company.

"We sought to do this in private and do this in a respectful way," he said.

"We'll do everything in our power to defend that matter but we'll continue to talk to Landbridge to try and resolve this."

Landbridge launched international legal action against the federal government over Darwin port earlier this month. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

In a prior statement, Landbridge said it acquired the port "through a fair, open and competitive process" and "multiple Australian government reviews" confirmed there were "no national security concerns".

"Having engaged with the Commonwealth in an effort to reach a constructive resolution, Landbridge has regrettably been unable to achieve a satisfactory outcome through dialogue alone and is now taking the necessary steps to protect its legal rights," the statement said.

Mr Marles said the government would have "preferred" the legal dispute "had never happened".

" But you inherit the world as you find it and we are pursuing this in the most appropriate, prudent, and respectful way possible. "

In 2015, Landbridge signed a 99-year lease of Darwin Port. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

Uncertainty on new buyer

In February, NT treasurer Bill Yan said he hoped to see a resolution to the port ownership negotiations in coming months, emphasising the need for certainty.

NT paying 'millions of dollars a day in interest' to stay afloat The NT Treasurer Bill Yan outlines his plans for the NT's financial future, saying private investment will be key.

Mr Marles did not confirm whether the government had secured a buyer for the port or when the dispute might be resolved.

"I'm not going to speculate publicly, we are seeking to work this through in a respectful way with Landbridge," he said.

Landbridge was contacted for a response but a spokesperson said the company had no further comments.

'Unlikely' US assets in NT deployed to Iran

During his visit to Darwin, Mr Marles toured new facilities at the Larrakeyah barracks, including a new gym and mess hall set to open next week.

Last month, the government published the 2026 National Defence Strategy, which included up to $16 billion for northern base infrastructure at RAAF Bases Darwin and Tindal, as well as other bases in northern Australia.

Richard Marles visited the barracks' facilities in Darwin alongside federal NT representative Luke Gosling. (ABC News: Olivana Lathouris)

Mr Marles said bolstering Darwin's capabilities and assets was a priority.

"It is really a high national asset from a national security point of view," he said.

Mr Marles was unable to confirm whether US assets based out of the NT had been used in the conflict in Iran.

"I don't have the specifics on that," he said.

"I think it's unlikely but I actually don't know specifically."

World.title: AFLW's 2026 fixture to feature women's and men's double-headers
World.content:
AFLW will feature heavily on a jam-packed AFL grand-final weekend, with four matches scheduled in Victoria on the public holiday before the men's premiership decider.

The women's fixture, released by the league on Thursday, features six matches in Victoria around the men's grand final.

The league hopes to cash in on the Friday public holiday (September 25) in Melbourne by pulling in crowds after the traditional men's grand-final parade.

A women's double-header at Princes Park is the highlight, with Carlton hosting Richmond, and defending back-to-back premiers North Melbourne taking on Melbourne.

Geelong plays Hawthorn on the Thursday night, Essendon and the Western Bulldogs will host West Coast and Port Adelaide respectively on the Friday, and Collingwood do battle with GWS on the Sunday.

The men's grand final is on September 26, with no women's matches scheduled that day.

The Lions face the Kangaroos in a grand final rematch as early as round two. (Getty Images: Daniel Pockett)

As previously confirmed, the AFLW season will start when St Kilda host Carlton on August 9 as part of a double-header with a men's match between the clubs.

The remaining eight round-one fixtures will be played the following week, starting with a Hawthorn versus Melbourne match on the Thursday night.

Two more AFL/AFLW double-headers will feature in round one: North Melbourne versus Geelong, and GWS versus West Coast.

The fourth confirmed AFL/AFLW double-header is a Sydney versus Essendon women's match at the SCG in round two ahead of a Swans versus Kangaroos men's encounter.

"The inclusion of AFL/AFLW double-headers during the season crossover period will provide a unique experience for fans and clubs alike," AFL head of scheduling Josh Bowler said.

Brisbane hosts North Melbourne in an AFLW grand final re-match in round two, while Indigenous Round (rounds three and four) and Pride Round (rounds nine and 10) will both be celebrated across two weeks.

The season will again span 12 home-and-away rounds, followed by a four-week finals series, culminating in the grand final on the last weekend of November.

AAP

World.title: Coles investigates 'weird scratching' Apple gift card scam complaint
World.content:
Australian supermarket giant Coles is investigating concerns about tampered gift cards purchased instore, after a customer's social media video about "fraudulent" Apple vouchers went viral.

Melbourne-based illustrator Georgia Perry posted to Instagram last night, claiming she had bought four Apple gift cards worth $500 each from Coles in the inner-west suburb of Yarraville.

When she attempted to use the gift cards online, she found the redemption codes had been scratched out.

"They're all f****** fraudulent," she said in her social media video.

"No redemption code, but just like weird scratching and like glue where the code should be.

"Four out of four have the same thing."

Warning: this video contains coarse language.

Loading...

Ms Perry raised a complaint with the ASX-listed company, but told ABC News that Coles's initial customer response was "very lacklustre and uninterested and unaffected".

Ms Perry said she was refused a refund by store staff, with the company's head office later offering her one on Thursday after she made direct complaints to Coles and went public with the case.

"I have never purchased a gift card before and won't again," she said.

In a statement, a spokesperson for Coles said the company was "working closely with our supplier as part of our investigation into the gift cards involved". It also defended its customer service processes.

Global company InComm, which is understood to have supplied the gift cards to Coles, has been contacted for comment. Apple has not replied to the ABC's queries.

What happened to the gift cards?

Ms Perry said she bought the Apple gift cards at Coles on Tuesday night to purchase a new iPhone.

She said there was an instore offer to receive 20 times the usual Flybuys points when purchasing Apple gift cards.

"Sounds like a good deal, right?" Ms Perry told her Instagram followers.

"No, not a good deal."

Have you had issues with gift cards? Email our journalist on terzon.emilia@abc.net.au or em.terzon@proton.me

Gift cards for major brands like Apple sold in major retailers usually come as plastic cards that are glued onto a cardboard swipe. The codes to redeem the voucher appear once the card is pulled off the cardboard.

The paper cardboard on the Apple gift cards that hid the scratched codes on the card until it was taken off. (Supplied: Georgia Perry)

Ms Perry said she took the $2,000 worth of vouchers to the Coles check-out, where she purchased them and a staff member activated them. Activation is a step enforced to ensure people do not use vouchers instore without paying for them.

She went home and took the first card off the cardboard casing. Ms Perry then realised the one she had bought had "no code" and looked like it had been scratched or peeled off.

Ms Perry feared she had accidentally damaged the gift card, so she moved on to the next one she had bought. It had the same issues, as did the final two gift cards.

Ms Perry said she took the gift cards back to Coles but that the staff "could not care less", and said there was "nothing they could do apparently because gift cards are a third-party product".

" Wouldn't everything at Coles be a third-party product? Isn't all coming from somewhere for them to sell? "

Ms Perry also raised a complaint with Apple. She said its helpline asked her to send in photos of the gift cards, including serial numbers, which led her to realise these had also been scratched out.

"The last like three numbers on each card, I can't really see," she told social media.

Georgia Perry says she found the codes on the back of the card were also scratched. (Supplied: Georgia Perry)

Ms Perry then made a formal complaint to Coles, which the supermarket giant confirmed it received yesterday morning. It has defended its escalation of the case through its channels.

"Our customer care team responded within one hour of receiving her enquiry and has continued working with her to investigate the issue and work towards a resolution," a spokesperson said.

Georgia Perry says she'll never buy a gift card again. (Supplied: Georgia Perry)

Ms Perry posted her video last night. By this morning, it had amassed more than 150,000 views and hundreds of comments, including from people concerned about gift card scamming and consumer rights.

Today, at lunchtime, a Coles staff member left Ms Perry a voicemail, confirming a refund was coming.

Emails seen by ABC News indicate Coles is giving Ms Perry a refund, after the supplier of the gift cards "deactivated" the $2,000 worth and "returned the money to Coles".

"Therefore you are eligible for a refund," the email stated. "Once again, we sincerely apologise for the poor experience," it added.

Ms Perry said the refund was clearly because of the "pressure" on Coles.

ACCC warns consumers to check packaging

The ABC contacted the consumer watchdog, the ACCC, about the issue, asking if there was a known problem with gift cards in Australia and whether it had received complaints.

"They should raise this issue with both the gift card provider and the retailer," an ACCC spokesperson noted.

"Consumers are able to return such gift cards to the retailer they purchased from, providing proof of purchase, to seek a refund or replacement gift card.

"However, consumers may also need to provide the retailer with information from the gift card provider confirming that the gift card funds were redeemed fraudulently."

The spokesperson said, "Signs of physical tampering are not always present when there is gift card fraud."

"Consumers are encouraged to inspect the gift card carefully before purchasing to check for any signs of damage or tampering, as one issue that can indicate validity or redemption problems," they added.

Ms Perry said she did not think to take the gift cards off their cardboard housing before buying them.

She said she wanted to know how the gift cards were tampered with, and whether this occurred instore or before the product hit the shop floor.

"It's mind-boggling," she told ABC News, adding that the issue seemed "perplexing" and "quite sophisticated".

World.title: Mum wins WFH rights, late start for school drop off
World.content:
BusinessWorkplaceWorkplace Mum wins WFH rights, late start for school drop off Jessica Yun May 21, 2026 — 4:12pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A Sydney mother has beaten back an attempt to force her into the office twice a week, when the Fair Work Commission ruled she was allowed to work from home all but one day a fortnight, when she is allowed to arrive late to let her drop her children at school. The mother, who lives on the far northern fringe of Sydney, had previously worked entirely from home at her four-day-a-week job, which allowed her to avoid a 90-minute commute into her employer’s office in the CBD. Stock image shows a woman working from home, which the Fair Work Commission ruled was acceptable in this case. Getty Images But after her employer was bought by global real estate software group Reapit Employment Services, the woman faced instructions to work from the Sydney CBD office two days a week. The instructions cited an employee survey flagging “concerning disengagement” among staff. This month, Fair Work commissioner Alana Matheson found middle ground after “protracted and complex” negotiations broke down between the part-time training and support team specialist and Reapit.



She ruled in arbitration that the woman would be allowed to largely work from home under workplace flexibility laws that the federal government beefed up in 2023. The ruling follows another case from last year when a woman working for Westpac was allowed to work from home on the far southwestern fringe of Sydney, to let drop her children at school. In this case, since 2016 the woman had been working from her home in NSW’s Berowra Heights for her employer, which was purchased in 2023 by global real estate software group Reapit Employment Services. Initially, it was happy with the work from home arrangement, but in May 2024, Reapit told the woman to come into the office twice a week amid allegations she had been “combative” in online meetings, lacked engagement with the broader team and was a negative influence. While never in the office, she had gone to a social lawn bowls event, the company allegedly claimed. Since 2024, staff had been required to work at least partly from the office to integrate the woman’s employer into the wider Reapit business. The woman responded by filing a flexible working request asking to “either work from home, attend the office fortnightly on a Monday, or be required in the office from 10am” to accommodate for school drop-offs and the 1.5-hour commute to the Sydney CBD office from her Berowra Heights home.



“I am the parent of a 4-year-old who I am responsible for getting to daycare, which is only open from 7.30am, and I am also responsible for getting my 7-year-old to school,” the woman stated. “My daughter has been diagnosed with [various conditions] over the last 12 months and can require additional support around drop-offs. Driving to the office would take me around 1 hour and 20 minutes, and public transport timing is similar.” Following this, Reapit approved a change in work arrangements that allowed the woman to work between 10am and 6pm on the days she worked from the office so she could do the children’s drop-off. “For avoidance of doubt, I have no issues with your productivity or quality of work,” said a Reapit representative. “As I explained, our hybrid working policy is a regional directive and the adoption of this is in no way related to your output.” After multiple negotiations for the mother to trial various arrangements failed to stick, Reapit granted a six-month exemption in November allowing her to work fully remotely, on the condition that the arrangement would be reviewed every six months.



Between mid-January and late February 2025, the company put the woman on a temporary performance improvement plan, requiring that she “actively promote positivity by refraining from spreading negative sentiment”. “Don’t ask questions on behalf of other staff members”, the performance plan stated. “Be a positive member of the team to promote team cohesion”. But in June 2025, despite the woman arguing she had been able to work from home without performance issues, Reapit deemed the arrangement unsuitable and said she would have to work one day a week in the office from July and August. The woman asked for this to be reconsidered. Her boss said she had done a “wonderful” job, in a document submitted to the commission. “[She] adds a lot of value to the team with considered feedback and suggestions,” her team leader wrote. But the mother’s request was declined because, Reapit said, it would lower efficiency and impact company culture and cohesion across the business.



Related Article Tax deductions Work from home tax claims restricted after ATO court victory Four days later, the woman notified Reapit that she would be taking the matter to the Fair Work Commission. Ultimately, commissioner Matheson ruled that the woman was permitted to keep working from home, citing her drop off responsibilities, but had to work from the office once a fortnight on a day of her choosing. To accommodate the special needs school drop-off and the long commute, the woman was permitted to start as late as 10:30am on the day she works from the office, but was legally obligated to make these hours up across the rest of the fortnight. The new arrangement will take effect from June 8. Reapit has been contacted for comment. The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion. World.title: ‘Unacceptable’: Israeli envoy summoned as ‘shocking’ footage sparks global fury
World.content:
Israel’s ambassador to Australia has been hauled before the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade to reinforce the government’s displeasure with a video of Israel’s national security minister taunting detained flotilla activists, Foreign Minister Penny Wong has said. In a Thursday morning statement, Wong said the provocative video of Itamar Ben-Gvir was “shocking and unacceptable” and that Australia’s ambassador to Israel had made Labor’s frustrations clear to the Israeli government. Loading “The images we have seen posted by Israeli Minister Ben-Gvir – who Australia has sanctioned – are shocking and unacceptable. We condemn his actions and the degrading actions of Israeli authorities towards those detained,” Wong said. The government has called for all detained Australians travelling on the Global Sumud Flotilla to be released and for Israel to comply with international obligations to treat detainees respectfully.



This is the second time Israel’s ambassador to Australia has been called in, after the previous ambassador Amir Maimon was summoned amid accusations of starvation and famine-like conditions in Gaza last July. The new ambassador, Hillel Newman, met with DFAT officials around 3pm on Thursday afternoon. The Israeli embassy in Canberra was contacted for comment. Shocking scenes from the footage released by Israel’s National Security Minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir. X/@itamarbengvir The video depicted Ben-Gvir taunting detained activists who tried to breach Israel’s blockade of Gaza, and telling them they should face lengthy imprisonment. It was condemned by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, triggering international backlash. Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni was among the most vocal critics, calling the behaviour a “violation of human dignity” and summoning Israel’s ambassador to Rome. The US ambassador to Israel and strong supporter of the nation’s settler movement, Mike Huckabee, called Ben-Gvir’s actions “despicable”, saying he had “betrayed the dignity of his nation”.



Netanyahu said that although Israel has every right to stop “provocative flotillas of Hamas terrorist supporters”, the way Ben-Gvir dealt with the activists was “not in line with Israel’s values and norms”. The message was echoed by the Australia Israel & Jewish Affairs Council, the Executive Council of Australian Jewry and the Zionist Federation of Australia. Ben-Gvir was filmed walking among some of the approximately 430 detained activists, a group that includes 11 Australians. In one, activists with their hands tied behind their backs are kneeling, their heads touching the floor inside what appears to be a makeshift detention area and on the deck of a ship. “Welcome to Israel, we are the landlords,” says Ben-Gvir, waving a large Israeli flag. One handcuffed activist shouts “free Palestine” and is immediately pushed to the ground by security personnel as Ben-Gvir walks by. Loading In another video, Ben-Gvir says the activists “came here all full of pride like big heroes. Look at them now”, while appealing to Netanyahu to grant him permission to imprison them.





“The legal team is in constant communication with DFAT, but unfortunately, both the legal team and the Australian family members, we’re still in the dark,” Bernadette Zaydan, a lawyer representing the majority of the Australian participants, said. “We know that there are some serious injuries that have been sustained by some of the participants, but we don’t know if any Australians were affected.” Related Article Israeli-Palestinian conflict The government has warned Juliet and her daughters not to join this group. They’re going to anyway Netanyahu has given instructions for the activists to be deported “as soon as possible”, The Legal Centre for Arab Minority Rights In Israel accused the nation’s authorities of “employing a criminal policy of abuse and humiliation against activists”, arguing that Israel had faced “zero accountability” for its actions against subsequent flotilla missions.



Flotilla organisers claimed Israeli soldiers fired on five boats during their interception, causing some damage. Israel’s Foreign Ministry said no live ammunition was fired and that “non-lethal means” were aimed at the vessels as a warning, but without targeting or injuring protesters. Israeli forces intercepted the flotilla, which set off from Turkey last week, about 268 kilometres off the Gaza coastline, according to the flotilla’s website.
